questions.text:
At a large school, 55% of students cycle to school. On any given day, each student independently decides how to commute.

A team of 8 students is selected at random.

(i) State why this situation can be modelled by a binomial distribution.
(ii) Calculate the probability that exactly 5 of the 8 students cycle to school.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: (i) Binomial because: fixed number of trials (n = 8), two outcomes (cycle/don't cycle), constant probability (p = 0.55), independent trials. (ii) P(X = 5) = C(8,5) × 0.55⁵ × 0.45³ = 56 × 0.05033 × 0.09113 = 0.2568. Accept 0.257.

questions.text: The school bike rack has spaces for 160 bikes. On a typical day, 250 students are at school. What is the expected number of students who cycle, and what is the standard deviation?
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Expected value: E(X) = np = 250 × 0.55 = 137.5 students. Standard deviation: σ = √(np(1 – p)) = √(250 × 0.55 × 0.45) = √61.875 ≈ 7.87.

questions.text: Using your answers from Question 1b and a normal approximation, estimate the probability that the car park will be full (more than 160 students cycle). Assume the number of students who cycle is approximately normally distributed.
questions.markingGuide: Merit: Need P(X > 160) where X = number of students who cycle. Using normal approximation X ~ N(137.5, 7.87²): z = (160 – 137.5)/7.87 = 22.5/7.87 ≈ 2.86. P(Z > 2.86) ≈ 0.0021 (≈ 0.2%). With continuity correction: z = (160.5 – 137.5)/7.87 ≈ 2.92, giving P ≈ 0.0018. Either approach acceptable. Must show clear working using the normal distribution.

questions.text:
Events X and Y are such that P(X) = 0.35, P(Y) = 0.5, and P(X ∪ Y) = 0.675.

(i) Find P(X ∩ Y).
(ii) Find P(X | Y).
(iii) Are X and Y independent? Justify your answer.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: (i) P(X ∪ Y) = P(X) + P(Y) - P(X ∩ Y), so 0.675 = 0.35 + 0.50 - P(X ∩ Y), P(X ∩ Y) = 0.175. (ii) P(X | Y) = P(X ∩ Y)/P(Y) = 0.175/0.50 = 0.35. (iii) P(X | Y) = 0.35 = P(X), so X and Y ARE independent. Alternatively: P(X) × P(Y) = 0.35 × 0.50 = 0.175 = P(X ∩ Y).

questions.text:
Events R and S are mutually exclusive with P(R) = 0.25 and P(S) = 0.35.

(i) Explain why mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities cannot be independent.
(ii) Find P(R | S).
questions.markingGuide: Merit: (i) If R and S are mutually exclusive, P(R ∩ S) = 0. For independence, we need P(R ∩ S) = P(R) × P(S) = 0.25 × 0.35 = 0.0875. Since 0 ≠ 0.0875, they cannot be independent. Intuitively: if one event occurs, the other definitely cannot, so knowing one occurred gives information about the other. (ii) P(R | S) = P(R ∩ S)/P(S) = 0/0.35 = 0.

questions.text:
A delivery service finds that the number of orders arriving per hour follows a Poisson distribution with a mean of 12 orders per hour.

(i) Calculate the probability of receiving exactly 9 orders in a given hour.
(ii) Calculate the probability of receiving 2 or fewer orders in a 15-minute period.
(iii) The company has capacity to process 16 orders per hour. Find the probability that demand exceeds capacity in any given hour.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: (i) P(X = 9) = e⁻¹² × 12⁹/9! ≈ 0.0874 (from tables or calculator). Merit: (ii) In 15 min, λ = 3. P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2) = e⁻³(1 + 3 + 4.5) = 0.0498 × 8.5 = 0.4232. Excellence: (iii) P(X > 16) = 1 - P(X ≤ 16). Using Poisson tables with λ = 12: P(X ≤ 16) ≈ 0.8987, so P(X > 16) ≈ 0.1013 (about 10%).
